# Upasīvamāṇavapucchā (Snp 5.7 (PTS Snp 205))

**ID:** Snp 5.7 (PTS Snp 205)
**Section:** Suttanipāta (snp)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-2
**Title (Pali):** Upasīvamāṇavapucchā
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0505m.mul4.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Upasīvamāṇavapucchā* is the seventh discourse of the *Pārāyaṇavagga* in the *Suttanipāta* (Snp 5.7, verses 1069–1076; PTS Snp 205) [Norman 1997-2001; Gómez 1976]. The text comprises an eight-verse dialogue between the student Upasīva and the Buddha, composed primarily in the archaic Triṣṭubh metre, with the opening verse in mixed Triṣṭubh/Jagatī [Norman 1997-2001; Wynne 2007]. In the dialogue, Upasīva asks what support (*ārammaṇa*) one must rely upon to cross the great flood of craving [Wynne 2007]. The Buddha instructs him to overcome the flood by mindfully contemplating nothingness (*ākiñcañña* / *ākiñcaññāyatana*), relying on the awareness that "there is not" (*natthi*), abandoning sensual desires, and watching day and night for the destruction of thirst [Norman 1997-2001; Gómez 1976; Wynne 2007].

When Upasīva inquires whether an emancipated person ceases to exist or remains eternally free from disease, the Buddha responds with the classic simile of the flame: just as a flame blown out by the force of the wind goes to rest and can no longer be defined (*na upeti saṅkhaṃ*), so the sage freed from name-and-form (*nāmakāya*) goes beyond reckoning [Norman 1997-2001; Pande 1974; Priestley 1999]. Verse 1076 serves as a locus classicus for early Buddhist apophatic thought: for one who has gone to rest there is no measure (*atthamgatassa na pamāṇam atthi*), and when all phenomena (*dhammā*) are eliminated, all pathways of speech are also eliminated [Buswell 1985; Pande 1974]. Modern scholars have noted thematic parallels between this dialogue and the *Aggivacchagotta Sutta* regarding the status of the liberated person [Pande 1974; Priestley 1999; Wynne 2007], as well as its relevance for understanding early conceptions of the cessation of perception (*saññā*) and proto-Mādhyamika perspectives [Gómez 1976; Pande 1974].
